title: Pride of birth
hook: a proud young brahmin insults the Sakyans, and his own ancestry comes out

segments.voice: Yesterday: the king's regret, and your line, regret, confessed. Did you offer an apology without an excuse? Today ends a week, with a young man very proud of his family. Day five hundred thirty-two.

A famous brahmin teacher named Pokkharasati wants to know if the Buddha is really who people say. So he sends his best student, Ambattha, a young man who has mastered the Vedas. Ambattha arrives and doesn't sit down. He walks around while the Buddha sits, talking at him. And when the Buddha asks if that's how he speaks to elders, Ambattha starts on the Sakyans, the Buddha's own clan. Once, he says, I went to their assembly hall in Kapilavatthu, and they laughed, and nobody offered me a seat. They're menials. Today: pride of birth.
screen: `POKKHARASATI SENDS HIS STUDENT.` → `AMBATTHA WON'T SIT DOWN.` → `THE SAKYANS LAUGHED AT ME.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's first reply is gentle. Even a little quail, he says, can chirp as it likes in its own nest. Kapilavatthu is the Sakyans' home. But Ambattha insults them again, and again. So the Buddha asks him a simple question: what's your clan? Kanhayana, says Ambattha. And the Buddha tells the old story. The Sakyans trace their line to an ancient king, Okkaka. That king had a slave woman, and she had a son named Kanha. Ambattha's clan descends from him. In other words, by the standards Ambattha himself has been using, his own ancestor was the son of a slave in the Sakyans' royal house. Ambattha won't answer at first. The text says a spirit holding a thunderbolt appeared above him, and he finally admits: yes, that's what my teachers say. His fellow students start jeering. And here's the turn. The Buddha stops them. Don't look down on Ambattha, he says. That Kanha became a great sage, and a king gave him his own daughter in marriage. So the story doesn't end as a humiliation. Read this way, it shows that pride of birth falls apart when you look closely. The Pali word is jati: birth. And then the teaching. In the highest knowledge and conduct, the Buddha says, there's no talk of birth, no talk of clan, no talk of who is worthy of whom. That talk belongs to marriages and family arrangements. Look back at the week: the moonlit ride, the dodging answers, honored, wings, the gem and thread, regret confessed. And now a family tree, shaken.
screen: `A QUAIL CHIRPS IN ITS OWN NEST` · `WHAT'S YOUR CLAN?` · `DON'T LOOK DOWN ON HIM` · `NO TALK OF BIRTH AT THE SUMMIT` · then, large: `PRIDE OF BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one pride of family. Everyone has one, quiet or loud. Our people, our name, our side of town, our school. Bring yours to mind, gently. Notice the small lift it gives. Now picture the family tree going back far enough, past anyone you know, to people of every kind. Let the lift soften. You don't have to stop loving your family. Just set down the ranking. The bell holds the time.
Pride of birth. Jati, birth, which matters to marriages and family trees, and not at all to knowledge and good conduct. Today's word.
Your line: pride of birth. Today, when you catch yourself sizing someone up by where they come from, look at what they do instead. Day five hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: In Buddhist monastic communities, people from every background ordain together, and order is counted from ordination, not birth; the teaching that conduct, not lineage, makes a person noble is repeated across the discourses.

myth: the Buddha tells the story of Kanha to humiliate Ambattha
when the other students jeer, he stops them and says Kanha became a great sage.
the Buddha first answers with the image of a quail in its own nest
the Sakyans were at home in Kapilavatthu, free to act as they liked.

fork.setup: Ambattha has finally admitted his clan's ancestry, and his fellow students are jeering at him. you're the Buddha. what do you do?
options: tell them not to look down on him, and praise his ancestor.
join in to drive the lesson home.
fork.reveal: the Buddha defends him: Kanha became a great sage, and a king gave him his daughter. the point was the emptiness of pride, not Ambattha's shame.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit jati: birth, also the group one is born into. the ground of Ambattha's pride.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha simply out-argued a rude young man.
what it means: he showed that pride of birth falls apart when traced back, and then defended the young man from mockery.

what a scholar hears: the Ambattha Sutta preserves an origin story of the Sakyans from King Okkaka (Ikshvaku), and its closing verse ranks knowledge and conduct above all lineage among gods and humans.

notes: DN 3 paraphrased. Confirm: Ambattha walking while the Buddha sits; the Kapilavatthu assembly-hall complaint; the quail simile; the clan name Kanhayana; Okkaka's slave woman (Disa) and her son Kanha; the yakkha Vajirapani with the thunderbolt; the Buddha restraining the students' jeering; Kanha's marriage to King Okkaka's daughter.

The discourse is a conversation within its own time about birth and status; it should not be framed as a judgment on Hindu tradition today. A Keeper may also wish a Hindu studies reader to check tone.

The Buddha's motive in telling the Kanha story is softened to a reading ('read this way'); the sutta itself has him press Ambattha hard. The script also omits the later section where the Buddha argues that khattiyas rank above brahmins by lineage; a Keeper should confirm that leaving it out is a fair simplification and not a distortion.
